\subsection{Platforms}
\draftnote{Reference fleet (docs/hardware.md): Clearpath Husky with a Velodyne VLP-16 and
RealSense D435i; Tarot 680 hexacopter with a D435i, a Cube autopilot (PX4) and a Jetson Nano, to
which a VLP-16 is being added (decision D6); BlueROV2 with a
Water Linked DVL A50, Tritech Micron Gemini 720s and Blue Robotics Ping360 scanning sonar; quay-side gateway bridging a 5\,GHz Wi-Fi
mesh and Water Linked M64 acoustic modems (64\,bit/s). The BlueROV2 tether never carries
Avatar traffic.}

\subsection{Setup}
\draftnote{Scenarios: Harbor, Dam face, Offshore jacket, Aliasing grid (docs/PLAN.md §6).
Teams: USV+2AUV; UAV+UGV; full. Tier-1 fast simulator; Tier-2 Gazebo Harmonic with
kinematic sensor rigs, a ray-cast sonar proxy (ADR-0007) and DAVE's multibeam sonar images
(ADR-0008); PX4 and Clearpath vehicle models are future work. Seeds 0--19 are the development
set, 20--79 are held out. Everything is simulation.}

\subsection{Baselines and metrics}
Independent single-agent SLAM; centralized oracle with ground-truth association; an
\emph{Above-and-Below}-style centralized server~\cite{mcconnell2026aboveandbelow};
Kimera-Multi~\cite{tian2022kimeramulti}, Swarm-SLAM~\cite{lajoie2024swarmslam},
SlideSLAM~\cite{liu2025slideslam} on air/ground subsets; DRACo-SLAM2~\cite{huang2025draco2} on
underwater subsets. Metrics: ATE with 4-DoF alignment~\cite{sturm2012tum, umeyama1991}, team ATE
in a common frame, frame error, association precision, bytes per link type.

\subsection{Results}
\draftnote{Tier-1 simulation, except the Tier-2 paragraph. Numbers are regenerated by
\texttt{make -C experiments paper-data} (Tier 2: \texttt{tier2}); tables are
\texttt{\textbackslash input} from \texttt{paper/data/}.}

Table~\ref{tab:server} compares \avatar{} with an \emph{Above-and-Below}-style centralized
server~\cite{mcconnell2026aboveandbelow} that receives the robots' keyframes (odometry and
detections) over the same links and budgets, runs the same association front-end and cycle
check, and solves one joint graph. The downlink is not charged, which favors the server.
With ideal links, the server matches the oracle, so any gap comes from the bytes and not from
the estimator. On acoustic links of 64--100\,bit/s the keyframe stream cannot keep up, and the
server rarely merges the AUVs, whereas \avatar{}'s condensed landmarks bring the whole team into
one frame in every run. At 1\,kbit/s the stream keeps up: the server merges the team, later
than \avatar{} and with slightly larger error. The server's failure case is instructive: with a small
fraction of an AUV's keyframes it can accept an aliased AUV--AUV alignment that no cycle vetoes,
which produces the large error at 100\,bit/s.

\paragraph{Correcting a drifting AUV}
\IfFileExists{data/drift_summary.tex}{\input{data/drift_summary.tex}}{}%
\providecommand{\driftSmallRuns}{?}\providecommand{\driftSmallMeanChange}{?}%
\providecommand{\driftTeamAte}{?}\providecommand{\driftNoScaleSmallRuns}{?}%
\providecommand{\driftNoScaleSmallMeanChange}{?}\providecommand{\driftNoScaleTeamAte}{?}%
\providecommand{\driftSmallWorse}{?}\providecommand{\driftSmallMaxWorse}{?}%
We claim collaboration only for small drift (Table~\ref{tab:drift}). A BlueROV2 makes a
one-way transit through the sparse outer harbor, and both ends of the transit lie in water
that another AUV surveys. Over the \driftSmallRuns{} runs whose solo drift stays below 1\,m,
sharing changes the drifting vehicle's error by \driftSmallMeanChange\,\% on average. The gain
is not uniform: some runs improve substantially, while in \driftSmallWorse{} the error grows, by
up to \driftSmallMaxWorse\,\% (Sec.~\ref{sec:discussion}). Metre-level
drift is not yet corrected (Sec.~\ref{sec:discussion}). Without the scale-error states of
Sec.~\ref{sec:system}, so that the simulated DVL and gyro scale errors go unmodelled, the
team ATE averages \driftNoScaleTeamAte\,m instead of \driftTeamAte\,m, and sharing changes
the drifting vehicle's error by \driftNoScaleSmallMeanChange\,\% over the
\driftNoScaleSmallRuns{} small-drift runs.

\paragraph{Perception in Gazebo (Tier 2)}

  \providecommand{\heldTwoAvatar}{?}\providecommand{\heldTwoRuns}{?}%

  \providecommand{\heldTwoEKFMedian}{?}\providecommand{\heldTwoMedian}{?}}
\IfFileExists{data/tier2_sonar_summary.tex}{\input{data/tier2_sonar_summary.tex}}{%
  \providecommand{\sonarTwoSGOne}{?}\providecommand{\sonarTwoSEKFGOne}{?}}
\IfFileExists{data/tier2_sonar_heldout_summary.tex}{\input{data/tier2_sonar_heldout_summary.tex}}{%
  \providecommand{\sonarHeldTwoSGOne}{?}\providecommand{\sonarHeldTwoSEKFGOne}{?}%
  \providecommand{\sonarHeldTwoSWrong}{?}\providecommand{\sonarHeldTwoSEKFWrong}{?}%
  \providecommand{\sonarHeldTwoSNNGOne}{?}}
\providecommand{\sonarTwoPEKFGOne}{?}\providecommand{\sonarHeldTwoPEKFGOne}{?}%
\providecommand{\sonarHeldTwoPGOne}{?}%
The same scenario is rendered in Gazebo Harmonic. Each robot is a kinematic sensor rig placed at
its ground-truth pose at every keyframe, with a VLP-16, a D435i depth camera, and a ray-cast
proxy for the imaging sonar (no speckle, multipath, or shadows). Odometry, depth, and ground
truth are those of Tier 1 for the same seed, so only perception differs. A geometric front-end
gates returns by medium, removes ground and seabed, clusters, and fits circles. Extended objects
such as hulls have no viewpoint-invariant centre and are mostly dropped. Table~\ref{tab:tier2}
reports \tierTwoRuns{} development seeds, on which every design decision was made, and
Table~\ref{tab:tier2held} \heldTwoRuns{} further seeds recorded afterwards. With ground-truth
intra-agent tracks, the team merges in every development run (\tierTwoMerged), an accepted
alignment is wrong in only \tierTwoWrong{} cases on the development seeds, and the frame error of
every robot stays below 1\,m (gate G1) in \tierTwoGOne{} development runs and \heldTwoGOne{}
held-out runs; the held-out exception leaves a BlueROV2 just above the gate. Team ATE is
\tierTwoAvatar\,m against \tierTwoOracle\,m for the oracle, versus \tierOneAvatar\,m and
\tierOneOracle\,m in Tier 1: the ratio to the oracle is similar, and the absolute error grows
because noisy clusters replace idealized detections. The proxy is idealized; sonar images follow
below.

Real robots do not know which detection is which, so the front-end must also associate
detections within one robot. A nearest-neighbour tracker that gates in the dead-reckoning frame
is not sufficient: G1 holds in \tierTwoNNGOne{} development runs and \heldTwoNNGOne{} held-out
runs (\heldTwoNNWrong{} wrong alignments held-out), because a BlueROV2's raw drift becomes
comparable to the spacing of similar piles; registering each keyframe to the track map first is
worse (G1 in \tierTwoRegGOne{} development runs). An extended Kalman filter over the robot's own
pose, its odometry biases, and the landmark positions, with their joint covariance, gates
detections against its own estimate, pairs the ambiguous detections of one keyframe jointly, and
lets a landmark inform the biases only after it has proved static. It reaches G1 in
\tierTwoEKFGOne{} development runs (\tierTwoEKFWrong{} wrong alignments) and \heldTwoEKFGOne{}
held-out runs (\heldTwoEKFWrong{} wrong). The median held-out team ATE is \heldTwoEKFMedian\,m
against \heldTwoMedian\,m for ground-truth tracks; the mean, \heldTwoEKFAvatar\,m, is dominated by one
run. Where it fails, the robot off is often the Tarot. Its depth camera sees a pile for
a few keyframes at a time, so between fixes its pose uncertainty is of the order of the pile
spacing, and a new pile is occasionally taken for a mapped one (Sec.~\ref{sec:discussion}); the UAV's
frame is then several metres off. The Tarot may also share only four or five landmarks with the
ground robot, and without the reverse-estimate test of Sec.~\ref{sec:association} the anchor then
accepted an alignment turned by about half a revolution, which moved every other robot by tens of
metres; with the test no such run remains. These counts are estimates: they move by about two runs
when the NumPy version changes, so the environment is pinned in the repository. The remedy is a sensor. With a light LiDAR added to the Tarot
(the optional upgrade of the fleet, modelled as a VLP-16-class unit), the same tracker, not
retuned, reaches G1 in \lidarTwoEKFGOne{} of \lidarTwoEKFRuns{} runs with \lidarTwoEKFWrong{}
wrong alignments (Table~\ref{tab:tier2lidar}), because the Tarot then sees many piles per
keyframe and can pair them jointly. The failure is mostly underwater with the simpler tracker
(Table~\ref{tab:tier2agents}): with it on the BlueROV2s alone G1 holds in \tierTwoNNUuvGOne{}
development runs, on the Husky and Tarot alone in \tierTwoNNLandGOne{}.

On the BlueROV2s, the ray-cast proxy can then be replaced by DAVE's multibeam sonar images
(speckle, reverberation and side lobes; Tables~\ref{tab:tier2sonar} and~\ref{tab:tier2sonarheld});
an image front-end extracts range-bearing blobs, and the other robots are unchanged. With
ground-truth tracks G1 holds in \sonarTwoSGOne{} development runs and \sonarHeldTwoSGOne{} held-out
runs (\sonarHeldTwoSWrong{} wrong alignments held-out); most failures leave a robot out of the
team (with more clique seeds the ambiguity test sees more competitors, and fewer teams merge than
with fewer seeds, but far fewer wrong alignments are accepted). The filter, tuned on the proxy, reaches G1
in \sonarTwoSEKFGOne{} development and \sonarHeldTwoSEKFGOne{} held-out runs
(\sonarHeldTwoSEKFWrong{} wrong alignments held-out). Its failures are mostly the BlueROV2 that
sees the fewest piles: between sparse fixes its pose is uncertain by about a pile spacing, the
filter starts duplicates rather than risk wrong matches, and the duplicates cost the loop closures
that keep its map consistent (Sec.~\ref{sec:discussion}). A second sonar addresses this: with a
Ping360 scanning sonar on each BlueROV2 (rendered by DAVE as four fans, of which each keyframe
keeps the sector swept since the previous one), the filter reaches G1 in \sonarTwoPEKFGOne{}
development and \sonarHeldTwoPEKFGOne{} held-out runs, against \sonarHeldTwoPGOne{} held-out
with ground-truth tracks; the full turn also shows hulls and the quay face, which the detector
does not yet reject. On sonar images, cross-medium association with ground-truth tracks mostly
holds; intra-agent association does not yet.

\subsection{Ablations}
\paragraph{Acoustic rate and digest order}
Table~\ref{tab:bandwidth} sweeps the raw modem rate (shared by the three acoustic nodes) for
three digest orders. Below a few tens of bit/s the team cannot merge within the mission. From
64\,bit/s up, the link budget, not the order, sets when frames connect; from 512\,bit/s to
10\,kbit/s the link no longer limits merging.

\paragraph{Packet loss}
\IfFileExists{data/loss_confirm.tex}{\input{data/loss_confirm.tex}}{%
  \newcommand{\lossConfirmFifo}{?}\newcommand{\lossConfirmQuality}{?}\newcommand{\lossConfirmVoi}{?}%
  \newcommand{\lossConfirmVoiFifoPairs}{?}\newcommand{\lossConfirmVoiFifoP}{?}%
  \newcommand{\lossConfirmVoiQualityPairs}{?}\newcommand{\lossConfirmVoiQualityP}{?}}%
Table~\ref{tab:loss} replaces the modem's range-dependent loss with the same packet loss at
every range. At 1\,kbit/s every team still merges at 80\,\% loss, only later. At the M64's
64\,bit/s merging fails as the loss grows from 40 to 80\,\%, and there the digest order matters.
In a test fixed before it was run (200 fresh seeds at 50 and 60\,\% loss, 400 paired runs), the
VoI order merged the team in \lossConfirmVoi{} runs and FIFO in \lossConfirmFifo{} (discordant
pairs \lossConfirmVoiFifoPairs{}, two-sided sign test $p=\lossConfirmVoiFifoP$), but not
significantly more often than the quality order (\lossConfirmQuality{}; \lossConfirmVoiQualityPairs{},
$p=\lossConfirmVoiQualityP$).

\paragraph{Front-end errors}
Table~\ref{tab:realism} injects identity switches (a detection attributed to a nearby part of
the same medium) and clutter into every agent's front-end. Without a robust kernel the team
falls apart; a Huber kernel limits the damage at low error rates but not at high ones;
graduated non-convexity keeps the team at its error-free accuracy in every run. Errors that
persist for a burst of keyframes, at the same rate of wrong attributions, are absorbed as well.
What no kernel can repair is a missing loop closure: if the front-end gives every revisited
pile a new identity, the drifting robots lose their corrections, and with any kernel the team
fails in many runs, whereas missing half of the revisits costs little. The oracle keeps ground-truth association and is not shown.

\begin{table}[t]
  \centering
  \caption{Team ATE [m] of \avatar{} under front-end errors (identity-switch rate + clutter
  per keyframe and sensor; ``in bursts'': a switch lasts 25 keyframes; ``split'': a part seen
  again after 30 keyframes gets a new identity) for three kernels on the landmark
  observations (Tier-1 simulation, 600\,s, M64, 20 seeds): median / mean; in brackets, runs
  that failed (the team did not merge, or its ATE exceeds 1\,m).}
  \label{tab:realism}
